segments.title: Name, birthplace and birth date
segments.summary: Burke Stevenson gives his name and says he was born in Louisiana on 14 April 1899.

segments.title: Father Boyle Stevenson and the country brass band
segments.summary: His father played cornet in a plantation brass band with relatives, taught by Professor Jim Humphrey; his father died around the First World War when Burke was about 15.

segments.title: Learning trumpet from Chris Kelly and leading his own bands
segments.summary: Kelly taught him trumpet from about 1918, took him on parades including Zulu; Stevenson bought his own horn, formed a band at 21, then a touring band in Mississippi.

segments.title: WPA-era band and the Kingfish Cabaret on Decatur Street
segments.summary: During WPA days he played with George Lewis and others at the Kingfish Cabaret and rehearsed in the large WPA band.

segments.title: WPA band outside jobs, pay and hours
segments.summary: The WPA musicians could take outside jobs; Decatur Street work paid decently in the Depression and ran late into the night.

segments.title: Switching from trumpet to bass at the Gypsy Tea Room
segments.summary: He played second trumpet at the Gypsy Tea Room, was asked to learn bass because players were scarce, and from about 1936 played with several bands before Kid Thomas.

segments.title: Personnel of Kid Rena's band
segments.summary: He lists the sidemen in the band including guitar, piano, alto saxophone and drums, with himself on bass.

segments.title: Hearing Bunk Johnson and Emanuel Perez
segments.summary: He barely remembers Bunk Johnson but knew his records; he heard Perez often on parades and at the roof garden.

segments.title: King Oliver, Louis Armstrong and the Royal Garden on Rampart Street
segments.summary: He remembers Oliver taking young Armstrong on parades, a raid on the Royal Garden after which Louis took over the band, and the band's lineup.

segments.title: Manuel Perez's pianist in the Oliver band
segments.summary: Asked about Manuel Moneta, Stevenson thinks he played piano with that band.

segments.title: Playing with Kid Punch and Lee Collins on parades
segments.summary: He played trumpet in Punch's band and with Lee Collins on parades, naming the trombone, clarinet and banjo players; parade bands were made up.

segments.title: Lee Collins's style and Buddy Petit
segments.summary: Collins played in the style of Buddy Petit, whom Stevenson praises as a fine second trumpet player.

segments.title: Never played with Petit; Sam and Isaiah Morgan bands
segments.summary: He never played with Petit but did with Rena, Kelly and the Morgans; Isaiah took over after Sam was paralyzed; he had his own band under his name.

segments.chapter: Chris Kelly and the country bands
segments.title: Deer Range plantation brass band and its repertoire
segments.summary: He mentions having his own band, then describes growing up at Deer Range, coming to New Orleans at 14 or 15; the country band played marches and quadrilles for dances and picnics, mostly not ragtime.

segments.chapter: Chris Kelly and the country bands
segments.title: Chris Kelly: knowing him in the country, his cornet and Kelly's Blues
segments.summary: Kelly was much older; he played a short cornet with mute and plunger, famously drawing a crowd with a blues played from the dance hall window.

segments.chapter: Chris Kelly and the country bands
segments.title: Personnel of Chris Kelly's country and city bands
segments.summary: He lists the Robinsons and others in Kelly's country band and the trombone, clarinet, bass and drums of his city band, with no piano.

segments.title: Never a regular in a brass band, hired by many leaders
segments.summary: He took lessons on arriving in the city but did not join a regular brass band; Kelly, Rena and others hired him as needed.

segments.title: Joining Kid Thomas in 1943 and quitting trumpet in 1936
segments.summary: He was with Kid Thomas about 15 years from 1943 and gave up trumpet completely in 1936 when he began playing bass.

segments.title: The best New Orleans bass players he heard
segments.summary: He names Albert Morgan, Ransom, Simon Moreira, old man Kimball, Jimmy Johnson and Bob Lyons as good bassists.

segments.title: Best trumpet players: Kid Rena, Petit, Kelly and Collins compared
segments.summary: He rates Kid Rena the best he worked with and contrasts fast-singing players with Kelly's slower style.

segments.title: High notes, Armstrong and Rena's clear tone
segments.summary: Collins played high at times, Petit never; Rena played above the staff, Stevenson thinks Armstrong got that from him, and Rena had the best clear notes.

segments.title: Wrapping up and arranging a return visit
segments.summary: They end the half-hour session, plan to meet again, possibly to record hymns and talk more about his father.
